title: Chapter 50: The Roof Garden, Part 2 of 5: Bridie's Sister
html:
She sat up against the wall, under the grating, and pushed Gideon's thin brown jacket off her shoulders. In the gray light her face was pale and creased on one side from the stone, and her eyes were very clear.
"How long have you been awake?" said Corin.
"Since fifty-one." She looked at Silas. "Good morning, Doctor."
"Good morning, my lady," said Silas, a little stiffly. He always called her that. He could not seem to stop. She had given up asking him to.
"May I see it?"
Silas gave her the notice. She read it the way she read everything, very fast and then again very slowly, her lips not moving at all. Corin watched her face while she did it. He watched it go still at Sweets will be given. He watched it go stiller at the round pretty signature. A. Pallister. He knew what she was seeing. Not the notice. A wide staircase on Crown Walk, at Midwinter, with lamps on every landing, and a thin pink smiling man in gold spectacles at the bottom of it with a little round silver box. Mr. Peppermint. That was what Rowan had called him, when he was small. Lyra had told Corin that on Monday, in the arches, in a voice like someone describing a dream they did not want to have again.
She read the two words at the bottom. Seen. Approved. She looked at the gray seal for a long time. Then she folded the paper in half, very neatly, and held it in her gloved hands in her lap.
"You're going up the Hill," she said to Corin.
"Yes."
"On that." She did not look at his leg. She did not need to.
"On something," said Corin. "I'll find something."
She was quiet for a moment.
"Rule one," she said.
Corin looked at her.
Rule one. It was the only rule they had. They had made it in the autumn, in Vespera's shop, on the floor, by candlelight, when he had still been a stranger to her and she had still been a girl with a forged letter and a dead scribe on her conscience. No lies between us. Not even the kind ones. They had both broken it since. He had broken it worse than she had. He had kept Elara from her for a week, and when he told her, on Monday, she had said That's not your choice what I carry, and he had known that she was right.
"I've got less to lose," he said slowly, "was a lie."
"Yes."
"I know it was." He looked down at the Ledger under his hand. "I said it because it was easier than the other thing."
"What's the other thing?"
Corin did not answer at once. Silas looked from one of them to the other, and then got up off the crate, very quietly for a man with such long legs, and went and stood in the arch beside Oren with his back to them. Oren did not look round. Gideon, on the floor, slept on.
"The other thing," said Corin, "is that I'm afraid. That if I sit here on this bench and wait for Monday, and do nothing, and they come down those steps at the seventh bell with their carts and their sweets, I'll sit here and watch them do it. Because I can't stand up. Because I can't fight. Because the only thing left that I can do well is the thing I promised I wouldn't do any more." He did not look at his hands. "And I'll do it. I'll burn something. I'll burn everything. I know I will. Malakor knows I will. That's why he told me not to, on Sunday. You won't stop. So I'd rather go up the Hill on Saturday, on one leg, and look, and find a way that isn't that. While there's still time to find one."
Lyra looked at him for a long moment.
Then she said, "Thank you."
"For what?"
"For telling me the real one."
She got up. It took her a moment. The gray gown was long and creased and her legs were stiff from the floor. She stood there in the middle of the vault, in her mother's silk, with her ragged hair and her pale face and the notice in her hand, and for a moment she looked like somebody Corin had never met. A tall woman in gray on a staircase, whom Oren talked about sometimes when he thought nobody was listening. Corin had never seen her. But he saw her now, a little, in her daughter.
"Then don't go alone," she said. "That's all. Don't go alone, and come back, and tell me what you saw. All of it. Not the kind version."
"I won't go alone."
"Who, then?"
Corin opened his mouth to say he did not know. And from the top of the crypt steps, out in the long hall, a woman's voice called down, loud and cheerful and very Lower Docks, the way it called down every morning at about this hour:
"Bread! Bread for the doctor, and for her ladyship, and none of it for that great lump on the crate unless he says please!"
And Oren, in the arch, said gravely, without turning round, "Please, Mrs. Kane."
Bridie Kane came down the steps with a basket on her hip and snow on her shawl.
She was a big square woman of fifty or so, with red hands and a red face and black hair going gray, pulled back so tight under her shawl that it made her eyebrows go up. She had a voice that could have stopped a cart. Corin had heard it stop more than a cart, on Friday, at the Fish Stairs, when she stood at the top of the steps and pointed at Silas's barrow with Corin lying in it and shouted FEVER at two hundred mothers, and the line broke, and the mothers ran, and half of them never took the sweets. Bridie was a step woman. She scrubbed the back step of the Bourse kitchen on weekday mornings, and Madame Hesper's back step on Wednesdays, and the great white steps of the Bank on Mondays and Thursdays. Or she had scrubbed Madame Hesper's back step. On Wednesdays. Until Thursday.
She had found Hesper. Oren had told Corin that. She had come in at the back door of the Needle and Thimble with the Watch behind her and found the old woman dead against the passage wall, with her shears in her hand.
She did not talk about it. She came down the crypt steps every morning instead, with bread.
She put the basket down on the end of Corin's bench, and pulled back the cloth, and the smell came up out of it, warm and brown and yeasty, so that Corin's empty stomach turned over. Four round loaves. Hobbses' bread, from the bakery at the bottom of Tallow Street, where the Hobbs girls took in Nell and Tobin. And a lump of yellow cheese wrapped in a cabbage leaf. And six eggs in a twist of straw.
"From Marta," said Bridie, and nodded at the eggs. "She says boil them. She says the doctor won't, because he forgets to eat, so somebody else is to do it and stand over him." She looked at Silas in the arch. "That'll be me, then."
"Thank you, Mrs. Kane," said Silas, without turning round.
"Don't thank me, love, eat." Then Bridie saw the paper in Lyra's hand, and her red face changed. "Oh," she said. "You've got one of them."
"Have you seen it?" said Lyra.
"Seen it? There's one on every church door from here to the Saltgate, my lady. And on the Fish Stairs board, and the pump on Tallow Street, and the door of the Bell. Nailed up first thing by a pack of little clerks with the Watch walking behind them. Notice of Removal." She said it the way she might have said a curse. "Well. It's not Saint Bride's on all of them. Saint Bride's is the only one with a number. The others just say any child found to be suffering. Any child. Found by who, I'd like to know?" She put her red hands on her hips. "I'll tell you by who. By a man in a brown coat with a blue badge on, and a bag of sweets, that's who."
Corin looked up at her.
"Mrs. Kane," he said. "Where does he go on Saturdays?"
"Who, love?"
"The man who signs them. Pallister."
Bridie looked at him. Then she looked at Lyra. Then she sat down, heavily, on the very end of the bench by the bread basket, so that the whole bench creaked and Corin's leg jolted on it and he had to shut his teeth.
"Funny you should ask that," she said. "Funny you should ask that, because it was in my mind to tell you, and I didn't know if it was any use. It's my sister Kitty. She does the steps on Linden Walk on a Saturday morning. Six houses. All the way down one side, nine till noon. She's done it nine years. And the narrow white one at the end, with the brass hand on the door, that's his." She nodded at the paper. "His. Pink as a sugar pig. Always says good morning to her. Always gives her a sweet, on her way out. She never eats them. She's got a whole jar of them at home. She says she doesn't know why she doesn't. She just doesn't."
"Sensible woman," said Silas from the arch.
"She is, Doctor. She's the clever one. I'm the loud one." Bridie looked back at Corin. "Well. Kitty says that on a weekday he goes out at the eighth bell, regular as a clock, in his carriage, down the Hill. To his office. To the Health. You can set your watch by him, she says, if you had a watch. But on a Saturday he doesn't go down. On a Saturday he comes out at the first bell after noon, every Saturday since the autumn, with his stick and his little silver box, and his carriage goes up."
"Up where?"
"That's what Kitty asked the coachman. He's a nice lad, the coachman. Bit simple. He told her. To the top, missus. Same as always. To the big house." Bridie leaned forward a little, and her voice went lower, which for Bridie meant that only half the crypt could hear it instead of all of it. "There's only one big house at the top of the Hill, love. Above the Crescent, above everything. With the dome on it like an egg in a cup."
Nobody said anything for a moment.
Out in the long hall, Mrs. Doyle had started singing again, softly, by the braziers. Polly's eyes, on the nearest pallet, were on the lamp.
"The Archon's palace," said Lyra.
"That's the one, my lady."
"Every Saturday."
"Every Saturday since the autumn. First bell after noon. Back down by the fourth." Bridie sat back. "And I'll tell you something else for nothing, while I'm about it, since we're asking. Abner Cole has the coal for that house. Has had for eleven years. Forty sacks a week, down the chute in the back lane, every Saturday at the second bell after noon. He's the only coal man on the Hill they'll let through that back gate, because his father had it before him and nobody's ever thought to change it." She looked at Corin's leg on the bench, and then at his face, and her red cheeks went a little redder. "I'm not saying anything. I'm just saying."
Corin looked at Lyra.
Lyra looked at him. And then, slowly, as if she could not help it, the corner of her mouth went up.
"Coal," she said.
"Coal," said Corin.
"You're going to go to the Archon's palace," said Silas, turning round at last in the arch, "in a coal cart."
"Nobody looks twice at a coal man," said Corin. "Bridie said so herself. On Thursday. Nobody looks twice at fever, and nobody looks twice at coal."
"I never said that," said Bridie.
"You will," said Corin. "When they ask you."
And on the floor by the arch, Gideon, who had been asleep the whole time, said without opening his eyes, "I'm coming."
"No," said Corin and Lyra and Silas, all at once.
Gideon opened one eye.
"Why not?"
"Because you've got no big toes," said Silas. "And you've got twelve stitches in your arm. And because your face has been in Pike's watch book since Sunday, and in the Lady's selling room since Tuesday, and there are two hundred people on the Hill who'd know you from the back." He paused. "And because somebody has to be here on Monday morning at the seventh bell, Gideon. Somebody who can count."
Gideon looked at him for a long moment with the one eye. Then he shut it again.
"Juno, then," he said into his knees. "Juno's got all her toes."
"Juno," said Lyra, and looked at Corin. "Rule one. Don't go alone."
"Juno," said Corin.
Coal
Juno came in at the eleventh bell, walking on the sides of her feet.
She had been out since first light with the step women, carrying the morning's news from door to door, the way she carried everything. She was fourteen, small and quick and sharp-faced, with a mop of brown hair that would not lie flat and a voice that never stopped. She wore three shawls, one on top of the other, and a boy's jacket over them, and a brass key on a string round her neck, under everything, that had been her grandfather's. Her feet were wrapped in strips of old blanket inside a pair of Mrs. Doyle's dead husband's boots, three sizes too big, stuffed with straw. Doctor Silas had looked at her feet on Thursday and said she would keep every toe if she stayed off them for a fortnight. She had not stayed off them for an hour.
"There's one on the Bank steps," she said, before she was even under the arch. "A notice. Bridie's furious. She scrubbed round it. And one on the door of the Bell, and Coker's sister tore it down and spat on it and the Watch took her name. And the gray-cap boy's not in the graveyard today. He's been moved. There's a new one. Older. Sitting on the wall by the lych gate pretending to eat a pie. He's been eating the same pie since the ninth bell." She stopped. She looked at Corin's face, and then at Lyra's. "What? What is it? Why are you all looking at me like that?"
They told her.
She listened with her mouth a little open. When they got to the part about the coal cart, she shut it.
"Up the Hill," she said. "To the Archon's. In Abner Cole's coal cart."
"Yes."
"With you." She looked at Corin's leg. "On that."
"Everybody keeps saying that," said Corin.
"Because everybody's right." But her eyes had gone bright, the way they went bright on a roof, at night, just before she jumped a gap that she should not jump. "Does Abner know?"
"Not yet," said Lyra.
"Then I'll tell him." Juno was already turning round. "He's on his round. Monday's Brindle, Saturday's the Hill. He loads at the yard at noon. If I go now I'll catch him at the yard." She stopped in the arch and looked back. "He'll say no."
"Will he?"
"He'll say no three times. Then he'll say the things I do for Hessa. Then he'll say yes." And she was gone, up the long hall, at a hobbling half-run on the sides of her feet, with her three shawls flying, before anybody could tell her to walk.
It went almost exactly as she said.
Abner Cole came round to the lane behind Saint Bride's a little before the first bell after noon, with his cart.
He did not come to the front. Nobody came to the front of Saint Bride's any more. The front of Saint Bride's was the graveyard and the lych gate, and the lych gate had a young man in a gray cap sitting on its wall eating a pie. So they went out the back way, which old Amos the bell-ringer showed them. Amos was very old and very deaf and had rung the bells of Saint Bride's for forty years by the Ministry's great bell across the river, because the church clock had stopped long before he came. He did not ask any questions. He could not have heard the answers. He just took a big iron key off a nail in the vestry and opened a low door behind the altar, a door so old and so small that even Juno had to duck, and stood aside.
Beyond the door there was a passage. Beyond the passage there were three stone steps, and a rotten wooden door, and then a lane.
Getting Corin to the lane took a long time.
Oren carried him. He did it with one arm, because the other was in the sling, and he did it without being asked. He just bent down by the bench, and put his good arm under Corin's back, and said Ready, sir, and stood up. Corin had not known that a man could lift another man with one arm. Oren did not seem to know it either. His face went dark red and the cords stood out in his neck and he did not make a sound. Doctor Silas held the bad leg straight, walking backward in front of them, step by step, all the way up the crypt steps and through the dark church and through Amos's little door, saying Mind. Mind. Mind the splint. Mind. And Lyra walked behind with the Ledger in her arms and the lamp held up, and said nothing at all.
At the rotten door at the end of the passage, Oren stopped, and set Corin down on the top step, as gently as if he were made of glass, and stood back, breathing hard.
"Thank you, Oren," said Corin.
The big man shook his head. He did not like being thanked.
The lane was narrow and dirty and full of snow, with high black walls on both sides, the back walls of warehouses. And in the middle of it, filling it almost from wall to wall, was Abner Cole's coal cart.
It was a long low flat cart, black with coal dust in every crack of its old boards, with two big iron-rimmed wheels and a high seat at the front and a pair of sideboards to keep the sacks from falling off. It was loaded with sacks. Coal sacks, black and fat and lumpy, piled up behind the seat in rows, four rows deep and three sacks high. There was a smell of coal and wet horse and cold. And in the shafts, standing very patiently in the snow with her head down, was a horse. A big brown cart mare with feathered feet and a white blaze on her face, and a nose-bag on, and a blanket over her back with the words A. COLE & SON, TALLOW ST. stitched on it in red wool that had gone brown.
Abner Cole was sitting on the seat.
He was a big slow broad man of about sixty, as black as his cart. Coal black. Not his skin, which under the coal was as pink as anybody's. But every inch of him that showed was black with coal dust, his face and his neck and his big hands and the bald top of his head, which he covered with an old leather cap with a long flap at the back, to keep the coal from going down his collar. His eyes looked very white in all that black. He wore a leather apron and a leather cape over his shoulders, shaped like a hood, that coal men wore to carry the sacks on their backs.
He looked down at Corin on the step. He looked at the leg. He looked for a long time.
"No," he said.
Juno, who was sitting on the sacks behind him with her feet in their huge boots dangling over the side, rolled her eyes.
"That's the third," she said.
"That's the fourth," said Abner. "I said it three times at the yard." He looked at Corin again. His voice was very deep and very slow. It sounded like coal going down a chute. "You know what they do, Mister Vane? Up there? At that gate? If they find a man in my cart who isn't meant to be in my cart?"
"No."
"Neither do I. Nobody's ever done it. Eleven years I've had that gate. My father had it twenty before me. Never once." He breathed out through his nose, and a little cloud of coal dust came out with it into the cold air. "That's what's worrying me."
Corin waited.
Abner looked at him a moment longer. Then he looked away, up the lane, at the gray sky between the black walls. And he said, quite softly, to nobody, "The things I do for Hessa."
Juno grinned.
"Get him up, then," said Abner Cole. "And mind my sacks."
They got him up.
They put him in the back, sitting on a folded sack against the back of the driver's seat, with his bad leg out straight along the boards between two rows of coal and his crutch beside it. Then Abner climbed down, and took a handful of coal dust off the floor of the cart, black and fine and soft as flour, and looked at Corin's face.
"Shut your eyes," he said.
Corin shut them.
Abner rubbed the coal dust into his face. All over it. Slowly and thoroughly, with his big rough thumbs, the way a man rubs grease into a boot. Into the hair at his temples. Into his eyebrows. Down his nose, round his mouth, under his chin, into the creases of his neck. It was cold and gritty and it smelled of the inside of the earth. When he had finished with the face he took Corin's hands, one after the other, and turned them over in his own.
He stopped.
Corin opened his eyes.
Abner was looking at his hands. At the gray. Dull pewter gray, from the tips of the fingers to past the wrists, going on up under the cuffs of his coat. The fingers stiff and half-curled. The skin smooth and cold and strange, like the skin of a statue.
Abner did not say anything about it.
He took another handful of coal dust and rubbed it into the gray hands until they were black. Black as his own. Every finger. Every nail. Up over the wrists and under the cuffs. Then he looked at them again, and nodded.
"There," he said. "Now you're a coal man."
Then he gave Corin his own spare cap, an old one, leather, with a long flap at the back. And a leather cape like his, cracked and stiff and smelling of fifty winters. And he climbed back up onto his seat, and picked up the reins, and looked down at Lyra and Silas and Oren standing in the snow in the lane.
"Back by the fourth bell," he said. "Or the fifth. Depending."
"Depending on what?" said Silas.
Abner considered this.
"Depending," he said.
And he clicked his tongue at the brown mare, and she lifted her big feathered feet out of the snow, one, two, three, four, and leaned into the collar, and the cart creaked and groaned and began to roll.
Corin looked back.
They were standing at the rotten door at the end of the lane. Silas with his arms folded and his long face set. Oren with his good hand on the wall. And Lyra in front of them both, in Gideon's thin brown jacket over her mother's gray gown, with the Ledger held against her chest in both arms. She did not wave. She just stood and watched him go.
Then the cart turned the corner at the end of the lane, and she was gone.
They went up through the city slowly.
It was a long way from Saint Bride's to the Hill. Down to the river first, along the old wharves where the snow lay gray and trodden over the cobbles. Then over the river by the Tanners' Bridge, which was old and narrow and humped like a cat's back, with little stone shelters at each end where the toll men used to sit. Then up. Up through the Ink Quarter, where the printers' shops had their shutters down for Saturday and the gutters ran black with ink and snow water. Up past the Ministry Steps, a hundred and twelve of them, white and wide, climbing to the great bronze doors with the words cut over them that Corin could not see from here but knew by heart. WHAT IS WRITTEN IS KEPT. Up into the wide streets with the shops with glass windows, and the cab horses with blankets on, and the ladies in furs, and the boys sweeping crossings.
Nobody looked at them.
Abner had been right. Bridie had been right. Nobody looked twice at coal. People stepped out of the way of the big brown mare without seeing her. A lady in a velvet cape pulled her skirts aside as the cart went past so that the black dust would not touch them, and did not lift her eyes. A Watch constable at a corner stamped his feet and blew on his hands and looked straight through them. Corin sat on his sack with his black face and his black hands and his leather cape round his shoulders, with his leg out along the boards between the sacks, and the city went past him, and did not see him at all.
It was very strange. He had spent all autumn being seen. Hunted, and looked for, and drawn on posters. WANTED. The Thorne Abduction. Aged about thirty. Gray marks on the hands. And now he was sitting in the open, in the middle of the afternoon, in the middle of the busiest streets in the city, and he was nobody.
Juno, beside him on the sacks, saw his face and grinned.
"It's good, isn't it?" she said under her breath. "Being nobody. I do it all the time."
They were stopped once.
At the bottom of Exchange Street, where it met the river road, there was a barrier across the way. A long pole, painted black and white, on two trestles. And beside the barrier, a cart of hooks. One of the six black carts Oren had told him about, full of long iron poles with hooks on the end, twelve feet long. And round the cart, in the snow, four boys.
Drum boys. Harlan Vance's drum boys, from Highmoor. Corin had never seen one up close. They were so young. The oldest could not have been fifteen. The youngest was smaller than Juno. They wore long black coats that came down to their ankles, buttoned to the chin, and flat black caps with a little white badge on the front, an open eye. On each boy's left hip there was a small square box of black leather. Their short swords hung on the other hip. Their faces under the black caps were red with cold and very serious. One of them had a drum on his back, on a strap. It was the only drum Corin could see.
The smallest boy stepped out in front of the brown mare and held up his hand.
Abner stopped the cart.
"Load?" said the boy. His voice had not broken yet. He was trying very hard to make it deep.
"Coal," said Abner.
"Where to?"
"The top."
The boy looked at him. Then two of the others took hooks off the black cart, the long iron poles, and came round the sides of the coal cart, one on each side, and began to poke the sacks.
They did it properly. Corin would remember that afterward. They did not just jab at the top row. They pushed the hooks in between the sacks, deep, all the way down to the boards, row by row, along the whole length of the cart, the way you would push a stick into a haystack to find a rat. Chock, went the hooks, on the boards. Chock. Chock. One went in between two sacks a hand's width from Juno's knee. She did not move. One went in by Corin's bad leg and he felt the iron touch the splint through the sacking, and the boy holding it felt it too, and stopped.
The boy looked at Corin.
Corin looked back at him from under the flap of Abner's cap, out of a black face, with white eyes.
"My lad," said Abner Cole slowly from the seat, without turning round. "Broke his leg Tuesday. Coal sack fell on it. He sits on the cart and minds the horse. Can't carry. Won't stay home." He spat over the side into the snow. "Same as his mother."
The drum boy looked at the leg. At the splints of ash wood under the sacking. Then at Corin's black face again.
Then he pulled the hook out, chock, and stepped back.
The smallest boy, in front of the mare, had been looking at something in his hand. A little brass disk that Abner had held down to him off the seat, on a chain round his neck. It was the size of a big coin, and very worn, and on the front of it there was a stone eye stamped into the brass, and under the eye the words SERVICE. THE PALACE. And on the back, scratched in by hand, a long time ago: COLE.
The boy's lips moved, reading it. He gave it back.
"Pass," he said, in his not-quite-deep voice, and stood out of the way, and the other two lifted the black and white pole off its trestles.
The brown mare leaned into the collar.
And the cart rolled on, up Exchange Street, past the great dark shape of the Bourse on the right, with its glass dome all white with snow, and its bronze doors shut, and two big men in plum-colored coats standing on the steps outside it, very still, one on each side, like the stone lions on the Bank.
Corin did not look at it. He looked at his black hands.
They had not shaken at all. Not once. Not at the barrier. Not when the hook touched the splint. He noticed that. He would remember noticing it, later.
